verifications.claim: The Artemis II Orion capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, California, on Friday, April 10, 2026.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "NASA’s Artemis II mission is scheduled to splash down off the coast of San Diego" (R1); "The Orion capsule has splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, about 40 to 50 miles off the coast of San Diego" (R2); "Splashdown is targeted for 8:07 p.m. EDT (5:07 p.m. PDT) off the coast of San Diego" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources directly confirm the exact location, date, and that splashdown occurred as planned.

verifications.claim: The Artemis II Orion capsule landed approximately 40 to 50 miles off the San Diego coast.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "about 40 to 50 miles off the coast of San Diego"; "roughly 40-50 miles southwest of San Diego"
verifications.reasoning: R2 directly states the precise distance off the San Diego coast.

verifications.claim: The Artemis II Orion capsule landed at roughly 8:07 p.m. EDT (5:07 p.m. PDT).
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "approximately 8:07 p.m. EDT (5:07 p.m. PDT)" (R1, R4); "8:07 p.m. ET" (R2, R5, R7)
verifications.reasoning: Exact time and time zones match across multiple sources.

verifications.claim: The splashdown ended a 10-day crewed mission around the Moon.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "approximately 10-day journey around the Moon" (R1); "10-day trip to the moon" (R2); "approximately 10-day journey that will take them beyond the Moon" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: All relevant sources consistently describe it as a ~10-day crewed mission around the Moon.

verifications.claim: Splashdown location was the Pacific Ocean near San Diego, California.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego" (multiple, e.g., R1, R2, R4)
verifications.reasoning: Directly supported by nearly all sources as the splashdown location.

verifications.claim: A joint NASA and U.S. Navy team including the USS John P. Murtha recovered the astronauts and capsule.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "teams from NASA and the U.S. military will extract the crew... to the USS John P. Murtha" (R1); "USS John P. Murtha, which was positioned... to recover" (R2); "USS John P. Murtha (LPD 26) is slated to serve as the recovery ship for the Orion spacecraft and its crew" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Sources explicitly name joint NASA/Navy teams with USS John P. Murtha for recovery of crew and capsule.

verifications.claim: The crew was retrieved via helicopter.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "recovery teams will retrieve the crew using helicopters and deliver them to the USS John P. Murtha" (R1); "successfully hoisted into waiting helicopters" (R2); "HSC-23 helicopters will recover the astronauts" (R3)
verifications.reasoning: Multiple sources confirm helicopter retrieval of the crew.

verifications.claim: The crew was taken to the USS John P. Murtha for initial medical evaluations before returning to shore.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "Once aboard, the astronauts will undergo post-mission medical evaluations in the ship’s medical bay before traveling back to shore" (R1); "flown to the flight deck of USS John P. Murtha... walked to the ship's medical bay" (R2)
verifications.reasoning: Exact sequence and purpose match source descriptions.

verifications.claim: The splashdown concluded the first crewed lunar flyby in over 50 years.
verifications.label: CLEAR
verifications.evidence: "first crewed test flight... around the Moon" (R1); "first crewed mission into deep space in more than 50 years" (R7); "first humans toward the Moon since 1972" (R4)
verifications.reasoning: Sources confirm it as the first crewed deep space/lunar mission since Apollo era (>50 years), involving lunar flyby.

verifications.claim: The spacecraft was expected to enter from the southwest.
verifications.label: VAGUE
verifications.reasoning: R2 specifies splashdown location as southwest of San Diego, implying approach direction, but no explicit mention of atmospheric entry direction.
